For families, the reality is far more severe: childcare costs have soared, and basic vehicle maintenance—such as a $100 oil change or a $1,000 set of tires—has become a significant burden, compounded by rising insurance premiums. Homeownership has become increasingly untenable, with mortgage rates, property insurance, and maintenance costs climbing steadily. Even everyday essentials reveal the truth: a simple loaf of wheat bread now costs $5.00, and both the quality and quantity of groceries have diminished while prices climb. Beyond the supermarket, the costs for streaming services, hardware, and travel have jumped by double digits. The government’s data simply does not reflect our lived experience, yet these outlets continue to print those figures as objective fact while we struggle to keep up.

The author wrote: "No technological improvement in the history of the world has ultimately failed to create more jobs than it destroyed."

That is incorrect. Technology has greatly reduced employment. In the 19th century, people worked from age 14 until they were disabled or dead at age 65. They worked 60 hours a week. Nowadays, Americans work 40 hours a week, but more importantly, they do not begin to work until they graduate from high school or college, they are able to retire at 65 or 70, living another 15 years. Overall, far fewer years of our lives are devoted to work. 

More to the point, my late mother was a social scientist at the Census Bureau. She said, "No trend lasts forever, or the world would be knee-deep in black and white televisions." In this case, the trend of eliminating jobs and finding new ones cannot continue indefinitely, because eventually we will run out of jobs. Demand for goods and services is not infinitely expandable. We cannot consume 14 meals a day or drive 1,000 miles in five different automobiles.

As a graduate student studying "bohemian enclaves," I researched Carmel’s history and wrote a dissertation about it twenty-five years ago. People have complained about the disappearance of local shops and cheap housing for a century, but especially after WWII.
It's worth noting that the people who originally made the place "bohemian," like the poet George Sterling and the writer Mary Austin, used Carmel to bolster their countercultural images as the town used them to market its real estate. In 1934, a John Reed Club sprang up in Carmel, led by Langston Hughes and Ella Winter. But the American Legion would have none of it and drove Hughes out.
By the 60s, the Crosby tournament brought in new celebrities. And after Monterey Pop, the “bohemian enclave” ran teenage hippies out of town. The public park’s sprinklers were set to turn on so often, Hippies couldn’t hang out or sell things they’d made to tourists. 
All the while, there were travel articles about how it was still bohemian though not what it used to be. Mayor Clint Eastwood, a local businessman, kept the story going. His Dirty Harry persona offered a countercultural, rebellious aura to the place. 
Carmel’s story of decline is California’s. The promise of an easy life and perfect climate hides the reality that many in Monterey County struggle to make rent. Just look at the bus stops in Carmel late in the day, when women of color, travel back to apartments in the low-income communities away from Carmel’s perfect beach.

A bevy of specialists suspected  Giant-cell Arteritis (whch can cause sudden, irreversible blindness), a brain tumor, an anyuerism, Fuch's Dystrophy and strabismus. An arterial biopsy, a head CT, a brain MRI and an MRA ruled all those out. I ultimately solved the mystery myself. I had recently lost a lot of weight, which can cause many body parts to sag, including the ear canal. My long-wearing, deep-in-the-canal hearing aids no longer fit well and had developed a whistling sound, particularly when my ear was covered, such as by a pillow. I'd been sleeping in a contorted position to avoid that, which created muscle spasms below my right ear, referring pain to my right temple. I started turning the hearing aids off at night. The whistling stopped. The muscle tension eased and the headaches went away.

comments.name: cory
comments.body: One of the main problems is getting to a CSF leak diagnosis.  First, because they can be discrete, finding a CSF leak can be difficult.  Second, and more important, is getting to someone who knows to look.  When my wife started experiencing disabling tinnitus we didn't know who we should see- ENT?, Neurologist? Radiologist? Pain Management Dr?  By a few wrong turns and a lot of lucky guessing we eventually got to a Neuroradiologist.  But even that wasn't easy.  Initially he thought it was an artery too close to the timpanic membrane and did a completely unnecessary and very scary surgery to close off the vessel.  It was only later that it occurred to him that it might be a CSF leak (a much more likely diagnosis).  He found a couple of leaks and plugged them, but missed a couple others.  The imaging is not that clear, so they are hard to see.  My wife is much better now, but getting from there to here was a labyrinth, even though my wife is a NP and I am a medically trained attorney.  Imagine the uniformed trying to navigate this.

It was eventually determined she had several spinal cord leaks, which were plugged in the fashion described in the article.  While this experience makes us wary of COVID shots, the main takeaway is that spinal cord leaks are grossly under-diagnosed and may explain many symptoms, particularly migraines.  But CSF leaks are not really on anyone's radar, and a lot of time, money and suffering are wasted treating symptoms.  The fact that it is mainly women who report such symptoms may explain it.

We need to really come to grips that we live in a New Normal. 

In Northern California, October 2017 was the time when everything changed. Emergency responders used to having hours to coordinate evacuations were overwhelmed and had no process to do so, nor accurate and timely information. Mutual Aid agreements collapsed when EVERYONE was fighting enormous fires. Rendezvous points considered safe bases for visiting departments were overrun and burned.

Already, we have many more tools. An excellent network of fire cameras. Night capable firefighting aircraft. Better communications and more delegation. Thank goodness for CalFire's fleet of aircraft, a bipartisan priority for decades.

But the air is dryer and the winds are fiercer and a firestorm like these can't really be fought, when embers fly a mile at a time. Blame is less appropriate than a serious rethink of what we expect a fire can do. We are alas on the cutting edge.

comments.name: David Sackman

Fire is part of the natural cycle of the brush and forests in California. There is supposed to be a fire every seven years or so in any particular spot in Southern California.  
But when fires are suppressed, which has been the policy in California since it was taken over by Europeans, the underbrush builds up beyond natural levels. “Fuel, not ignition, causes fire” explains brushfire expert Richard Minnich. The build-up of underbrush makes a fire not only more likely, but makes it burn much more intensely. In the natural cycle of fires, the underbrush is burned out every cycle, leaving the naturally fire-resistant native oaks and sycamores intact. But in the man-made obsession with fire suppression, the brush fire burns so intensely that it completely obliterates all the trees and everything else, in a horrific holocaust. 
he Native Californians practiced a complex system of controlled burns. This was not just primitive fire control, but a scientific agricultural practice. The burns were designed to promote certain plants and even wildlife.
Instead of respect for natural cycles, we have attempted to suppress fires entirely, treating fire as an enemy rather than as a natural phenomenon. We have introduced more combustible plants, like eucalyptus, to disrupt the natural balance. We have spewed carbon into the atmosphere, warming the entire planet, and changing the former climate cycles into something much more intense and unpredictable. 
Fire is not our enemy — we are.

I see my friends’ posts of smiling selfies and sunset scenery, and feel as if I need to rival theirs. When I first got Instagram, I realized everyone had this whole other life I never knew about. My piano teacher has an identical twin and my classmate of nine years is into photography.
What is shared to everyone is never what happened. A grainy shadow selfie shows that I was with other people, not that we stayed up past midnight laughing until our stomachs hurt as did our jaws. The memories exist only within the people. 
I post to create this image of me, but the girl making heart hands with her friends and posing with the drinks is not me. I am not always smiling, always with my friends. I just wish I was.
I think what you post tells a lot about how you wish to be perceived.

I'm a guy.  Hope no one minds if I barge in--

--and point out:  the quintessential "weird girl"--

--would be Medea.  Out of Greek and Roman mythology.  

I read that list of adjectives.  And what a list it is!  Words like "feral" or "obsessive" or "unhinged"--gosh, Medea!

--I think they're talking about you.  

Running away from your kingdom on the Black Sea.  Running away with Jason and his intrepid Argonauts--

--but falling out with the guy.  Or rather:  he fell out with you. And so (thwarted, thirsting for vengeance) you--

--but I'd better stop.  

The woman committed such crimes as even "weird girls" might shudder at.  

And who knows?  

Maybe those patriarchal bros from ancient times were incapable of handling an emancipated woman.  A woman unlikely to knuckle under--

--to the peremptory diktats flung in her direction.

And this too I remember.  

She was featured in a play by Seneca.  And her nurse (or someone) was expostulating with her. 

"Quid superest?" the woman cries.  "What remains?"   

To which indomitable Medea responds with a line that's rung down through the ages.  

                M E D E A    S U P E R E S T.  

What remains?  

               M E D E A     R E M A I N S.

And so she did.   But I'm glad I wasn't married to her. 

Ninety nine guys out of a hundred would say the same.  

And that hundredth guy?  

Don't ask! 

Thanks, NYT.

I'll never forget the screams on that flight, as well as the women saying the Our Father aloud while holding hands (myself included). The experience on this flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, though, was much worse. The wounded pilot's presence of mind in opening the cockpit door was a miracle. Speaking of divine intervention, as a practicing Catholic I've always crossed myself before takeoff, as well as when we land safely. I used to do it discreetly. Now I do it openly.
